sections.html:
A Jackson house carries tax from both the city and the county, and three offices share the work. Values come from the Madison County Assessor of Property. City tax is billed by the City of Jackson Revenue Office. County tax is billed by the Madison County Trustee. Nothing is paid to the Assessor, which also sends no bills. Sending a check to the wrong office only costs you time, so sort out which bill you are holding first: the city bill and the county bill are separate documents with separate payment points.

Find the Revenue Office at the west end of City Hall's ground floor, with weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30 and closures on national holidays. Take city payments to the customer service counter; for questions, the line is (731) 425-8212. The Trustee works out of Suite 107 at 100 E. Main Street, with doors open nine to five, and answers at (731) 423-6027. The Assessor is upstairs in Suite 304, reachable at (731) 423-6063 from half past eight to five.

City business licenses also come from the Revenue Office, so an owner renting out a Jackson house should ask whether one is required. The City Recorder holds ordinances, resolutions and any deeds the city owns, and the public can request to look at them.

Residential property in Jackson is taxed on 25% of appraised value. Multiply that assessment by the City of Jackson rate plus the Madison County rate and you have the bill. The county's online estimate tool applies the percentages in this table.

Assessment percentages used by the Madison County Assessor
Property classShare of value assessed
Residential25%
Farm25%
Commercial40%
Industrial40%
Personal property (net)30%

Treat the calculator as a rough guide; your actual bill controls. Rates change yearly because the County Commission and the Jackson City Council vote on them, so check the tool or phone the Revenue Office for what applies now. A county parcel outside Jackson might fall inside Three Way or Humboldt instead, and the tool lists separate rates for both.

The county's next full reappraisal lands in 2027, following the one in 2022 under Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-1601. In the years between, roughly one third of parcels get a field inspection annually to catch changes to land or buildings.

Madison County's median home sale price reached $251,450 in January 2026, against $212,500 in January 2022, an estimated 18.33% rise. A changed value triggers a mailed notice, normally in May; owners whose value stayed flat hear nothing. Many of these come back undeliverable, so phone the Assessor if you moved within the last two or three years.

  • Watch the mail in spring 2027 for a notice if your value changes.
  • Before any appeal, ask the Assessor to confirm the property record matches your house.

First, call the Assessor and have the property record checked. If the value still looks wrong, take it to the Madison County Board of Equalization, a five-member panel of local property owners. Hearings run on weekdays during the first two weeks of June, and appointments can be booked in the final two weeks of May.

You can contest only this year's value; 2025 taxes, for instance, are closed to challenge in 2026. If the county board rules against you, the next stop is the State Board of Equalization. File by August 1, or within forty-five days of the date on the county notice if that is later. The state charges a fee of $10 to $17, partly nonrefundable. Keep paying the undisputed portion on time so the account does not go delinquent mid-case.

What the Assessor wants to see:

  • Recent sales of comparable homes nearby, from the one or two years before the tax year at issue.
  • A recent paid appraisal.
  • Photos showing the outside and inside condition.

Applications go through the Madison County Trustee for elderly owners, disabled owners, disabled-veteran owners, and surviving spouses of a disabled veteran. The office asks for a driver's license, a Medicare card, a Social Security card, income proof covering the applicant, a spouse and all co-owners, plus a title or bill of sale for a mobile home.

A state property tax freeze program is also listed by the county. Relief pays you back after the bill is settled, so every bill must still be paid, and only a primary residence qualifies. Ask the Trustee at (731) 423-6027 when applications open.

Online city payments handle real property, meaning land and buildings, as well as personal property, meaning business equipment. A typical homeowner owes only the real property bill, found by searching a parcel ID or street address.

sections.h2: Selling a Jackson house with tax due
sections.html:
Expect the title company to request a payoff from the Revenue Office and another from the Trustee, since an in-town house has two bills. Call (731) 425-8212 for the city and (731) 423-6027 for the county. A house outside Jackson needs the Trustee only.

Once the sale closes, the buyer should have the Assessor change the mailing address, since both billing offices take addresses from that record. Missing your parcel ID? The city's payment guide explains how to search by street address in the public records tool.

A workable sequence for sellers: find the parcel ID, check whether the house is inside city limits, request a written payoff from each billing office, and give both to the closing agent. Do this early, because the Revenue Office and the Trustee keep different hours and each has its own phone line. Anything owed is subtracted from your proceeds at the table. In a cash sale the same payoffs apply, but there is no lender waiting on a long approval, so the tax figures are often the last piece the closing agent needs. Having both payoff letters in hand when you accept an offer keeps the closing date from slipping, and it spares the buyer's side from chasing two offices.

As the Madison County seat, Jackson lies 70 miles east of Memphis and 130 miles southwest of Nashville. It had 69,339 residents in 2025, compared with 68,205 in 2020, and 27,541 households. Owners occupy about 51.2% of homes. Median home value is $217,800, median gross rent is $1,145 a month, and median household income is $53,032. Nearly half of Jackson houses are therefore rentals, so some sellers will have tenants to deal with as well as tax bills. A landlord selling should also ask the Revenue Office whether a city business license on the rental needs to be closed out.

faqs.q: Where do I pay City of Jackson property tax?
faqs.a: Weekday payments are taken at the Revenue Office inside City Hall, and the city's online portal accepts real and personal property. Questions about city payments go to (731) 425-8212.

faqs.q: Who collects Madison County property tax?
faqs.a: The county Trustee takes payment at Suite 107, 100 E. Main Street, in Jackson. The office phone is (731) 423-6027.

faqs.q: When is the next property reappraisal in Madison County?
faqs.a: 2027 is the next countywide reappraisal year, after 2022. Notices of changed values come from the Assessor, typically mailed in May.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my Jackson assessment?
faqs.a: The Madison County Board of Equalization hears cases during the first two weeks of June, and appointments open in late May. Only the current year's assessment is open to appeal.

faqs.q: Does the Madison County Assessor send tax bills?
faqs.a: No. That office only sets values. Bills for city tax come from the City Revenue Office, and bills for county tax come from the County Trustee.
